questions.example: A secure protocol authenticates the parties and establishes a fresh session secret, then uses efficient symmetric encryption for the conversation.
questions.correct: Select encryption, signing, or authenticated key agreement according to the goal
distractors: All RSA use automatically provides forward secrecy
questions.goal: Explain RSA ECC signatures and key exchange in your own words, recognize a concrete example, and justify the matching protection or limitation.
questions.pitfall: Diffie-Hellman alone proves civil identity

questions.title: Signature verification from start to finish
questions.q: What does a recipient actually check when verifying a signed message?
questions.teach: The signature must match both the message and the trusted sender key. Verifying a signature is different from decrypting a message for privacy.
questions.answer: The sender signs a representation of the message using a private signing key. The recipient verifies the signature with a trusted corresponding public key and the received message. Alteration makes verification fail under the scheme’s assumptions. Signatures support origin authentication, integrity, and evidence of authorization/non-repudiation, subject to key custody and identity trust. A valid signature proves a key authorized the signed content; it does not automatically prove the content is true or secret. The textbook’s encrypted-digest diagram is a teaching model, not a universal implementation of every signature algorithm.
questions.example: Alice signs an invoice. If an attacker changes the amount, Bob’s verification fails. If Bob instead trusts an attacker’s substitute public key, he has not authenticated Alice.
questions.correct: Verify the received message and signature using the trusted sender public key
distractors: Decrypt the message with the sender public key to guarantee secrecy
Compare two untrusted plain hashes only
Use the recipient private key to identify the sender
questions.goal: Explain Signature verification from start to finish in your own words, recognize a concrete example, and justify the matching protection or limitation.
questions.pitfall: Decrypt the message with the sender public key to guarantee secrecy

questions.title: Attacks on cryptography
questions.q: How do ciphertext analysis, downgrade, weak algorithms, and bad implementation differ?
questions.teach: A strong mathematical primitive can fail in a system that exposes its keys or allows weaker options.
questions.answer: Ciphertext-only analysis looks for useful patterns without the plaintext. A downgrade pushes a protocol into weaker settings. Deprecated algorithms have known weaknesses or no longer provide an adequate margin. Misconfiguration or implementation mistakes can expose keys, misuse randomness, or apply a primitive incorrectly. Collision attacks seek two matching-digest inputs; preimage attacks seek input for a particular digest. The birthday bound for an ideal n-bit digest is roughly 2^(n/2), distinct from a roughly 2^n generic preimage search.
questions.example: A strong encryption algorithm does not help if its key is bundled in a public file. That failure concerns key handling rather than breaking the cipher mathematically.
questions.correct: Distinguish attacks on patterns, protocol choices, primitives, and implementation
distractors: Every cryptographic incident means AES was mathematically broken
Collision and preimage searches are identical
questions.goal: Explain Attacks on cryptography in your own words, recognize a concrete example, and justify the matching protection or limitation.
questions.pitfall: Every cryptographic incident means AES was mathematically broken

questions.title: File encryption full-disk encryption and hardware
questions.q: How do file encryption, disk encryption, TPM, HSM, and self-encrypting drives differ?
questions.teach: Choose what needs protection and where keys should be handled. Encryption hardware improves some boundaries, but it is not immune to every attack.
questions.answer: File encryption protects selected files or folders. Full-disk or volume encryption protects stored contents against offline access when keys are unavailable. A self-encrypting drive performs encryption in its controller. A TPM supports platform-bound key protection and measured-state uses; it is not simply a chip that encrypts all files or always refuses every altered boot. An HSM is a dedicated cryptographic key/operation boundary often serving applications or multiple systems. Hardware and firmware still require trustworthy implementation, configuration, and access controls. Recovery keys and backups are necessary operational considerations.
questions.example: A company may use disk encryption for lost laptops and an HSM for server signing keys. Neither prevents all misuse by an already authenticated running application.
questions.correct: Match protected data and key operations to the appropriate boundary
distractors: A TPM automatically encrypts every network packet
Hardware encryption has no possible vulnerabilities
File encryption always protects every temporary file on the disk
questions.goal: Explain File encryption full-disk encryption and hardware in your own words, recognize a concrete example, and justify the matching protection or limitation.
questions.pitfall: A TPM automatically encrypts every network packet

questions.title: Cryptography resource tradeoffs
questions.q: Why do low power and low latency affect cryptographic design?
questions.teach: Security work consumes energy, memory, and time. Small devices and fast-response systems must budget all of them.
questions.answer: Low-power sensors have limited energy and processing resources. Low-latency services must return results promptly. Lightweight cryptography aims to provide appropriate security within constrained environments; it is not permission to invent a weak cipher. Hardware acceleration can shift performance tradeoffs, but key management and implementation still matter. Evaluate the required property, threat, resource budget, and operational life rather than assuming the algorithm with the largest number is automatically the best system design.
questions.example: A battery-powered sensor needs authenticated readings without exhausting its battery. The design must protect integrity while meeting its power and timing budget.
questions.correct: Balance security requirements with energy, memory, processing, and response time
distractors: Hardware acceleration removes all key-management risk
questions.goal: Explain Cryptography resource tradeoffs in your own words, recognize a concrete example, and justify the matching protection or limitation.
questions.pitfall: Constrained devices need no authentication

questions.title: Stuxnet and misleading visibility
questions.q: What does the lecture’s Stuxnet example teach about targeted systems and monitoring?
questions.teach: The lesson is the combination of several attack paths and misleading observations, not a list of old numerical claims.
questions.answer: Lecture 1 describes Stuxnet as a worm targeting industrial systems, using multiple previously unknown vulnerabilities and removable-media entry, and altering equipment behavior while showing apparently normal readings. Use it to explain targeted cyber-physical impact, trusted-looking telemetry, and the limits of perimeter isolation. The lecture’s dates and impact estimates are historical course claims. For an exam scenario, connect removable-media policy, endpoint controls, segmentation, independent monitoring, and recovery.
questions.example: An industrial operator sees normal readings while physical equipment behaves abnormally. Independent evidence is needed before treating one display as complete visibility.
questions.correct: Targeted malware can combine entry methods with deceptive monitoring
distractors: Air gaps make removable-media controls unnecessary
Normal displayed readings prove the machine is healthy
questions.goal: Explain Stuxnet and misleading visibility in your own words, recognize a concrete example, and justify the matching protection or limitation.
questions.pitfall: Air gaps make removable-media controls unnecessary

questions.title: Choose the security device
questions.q: Which control best fits an IP block, a website category policy, or unapproved execution?
questions.teach: Begin with the requested action. Address filtering, website mediation, and local program execution are different enforcement points.
questions.answer: Lecture 2’s cases select firewalls/router ACLs or prevention for malicious connection sources; a proxy is the strongest course answer for blocking website categories; application allowlisting restricts unapproved programs. A passive IDS can alert but cannot itself guarantee a block. Host controls add visibility into local events. A packet sensor must actually receive the relevant traffic to observe it. Combine controls where the business case requires more than one kind of enforcement.
questions.example: A school needs to restrict gambling sites and stop unknown executables. A web proxy addresses the browsing policy; application controls address execution.
questions.correct: Choose enforcement by traffic attributes, application requests, or host execution
distractors: A passive IDS alone guarantees all blocks
questions.goal: Explain Choose the security device in your own words, recognize a concrete example, and justify the matching protection or limitation.
questions.pitfall: A passive IDS alone guarantees all blocks

questions.title: Detection tuning and business cost
questions.q: How do signature detection, anomaly detection, and tuning affect decisions?
questions.teach: Signatures recognize described patterns. Anomaly detection compares activity with an expected pattern. Both can be wrong.
questions.answer: A detection signature may be a byte pattern, behavior rule, hash, or other feature; it is not always one unique hexadecimal string embedded in the file. Anomaly detection may notice new behavior but can flag unusual legitimate work. A false positive can overload analysts or interrupt service when prevention acts; a false negative can let an attack continue. Tuning uses representative traffic and investigation feedback. Redundancy, scalability, and business needs constrain inspection design.
questions.example: A large legitimate backup suddenly triggers an anomaly rule. The team investigates and adjusts the rule without disabling monitoring for all other traffic.
questions.correct: Tune detection using evidence and business impact
distractors: A zero alert rate proves perfect security
questions.goal: Explain Detection tuning and business cost in your own words, recognize a concrete example, and justify the matching protection or limitation.
questions.pitfall: Every anomaly is malicious

questions.title: Defacement and advance-fee scams
questions.q: How do changing a website and a 419 scam differ in mechanism and business harm?
questions.teach: Defacement changes what a site displays. An advance-fee scam persuades a person to give money or information for a promised reward.
questions.answer: A site defacement may exploit a software weakness or stolen administrative credentials to alter public content, creating reputational and integrity harm. Defenses include safe configuration, updates, strong access control, restricted publishing privileges, monitoring, and restoration. A 419 scam builds trust around a claimed inheritance, lottery, or similar payout and then requests fees or sensitive information. Use independent verification and approved reporting, not participation in the claimed transaction.
questions.example: A changed homepage announcing false claims is a defacement. A message offering a large reward if an employee first pays a handling fee is advance-fee fraud.
questions.correct: Defacement attacks content integrity; advance-fee fraud manipulates trust
distractors: Both necessarily use the same database exploit
A defacement is always a harmless prank
questions.goal: Explain Defacement and advance-fee scams in your own words, recognize a concrete example, and justify the matching protection or limitation.
questions.pitfall: Both necessarily use the same database exploit

questions.title: Investigating an email without trusting it
questions.q: What evidence should you compare when reviewing a suspicious message?
questions.teach: Separate the message’s claims from evidence added by trusted receiving systems. A name, logo, or urgent story is easy to imitate.
questions.answer: Review sender/display name, sending domain, reply and return paths, routing hops, time/time zones, recipients, subject, and attachment/link context. Authentication results from a trusted receiver provide useful evidence but need interpretation. A mismatch or failed check can be significant; a pass does not prove the message’s business request is safe. Use known contact details to verify unusual requests. Preserve/report the original message according to the organization’s process.
questions.example: A message names a real professor but asks students to sign in on a lookalike site. The familiar name does not establish that the link or request is legitimate.
questions.correct: Compare trusted header evidence with claimed identity and request context
distractors: A display name proves the domain
A clean-looking body replaces header review
questions.goal: Explain Investigating an email without trusting it in your own words, recognize a concrete example, and justify the matching protection or limitation.
questions.pitfall: A university logo proves identity

questions.title: Fake antivirus and fake disk repair
questions.q: Why do professional-looking warnings still need independent verification?
questions.teach: Scareware sells fear. A convincing screen can invent an infection or disk failure to pressure installation or payment.
questions.answer: Lecture 4 distinguishes fake antivirus/rogueware and fake disk-defragmenter products. Both invent problems and request money or installation; installed malware may interfere with real security software or capture data. A polished interface and large scan count are claims, not proof. Use trusted support and already-approved security tools. If someone installed the product, investigate the endpoint and account activity rather than merely closing the warning.
questions.example: A website reports hundreds of disk errors and demands a fee. A page cannot establish that claim simply by displaying a scan animation.
questions.correct: Verify warnings using trusted tools and support before acting
distractors: A professional icon proves the product is legitimate
Every browser warning means the disk was scanned
questions.goal: Explain Fake antivirus and fake disk repair in your own words, recognize a concrete example, and justify the matching protection or limitation.
questions.pitfall: A professional icon proves the product is legitimate

questions.title: Controlled hardening and patch validation
questions.q: Why test small groups of hardening changes and verify the rollout?
questions.teach: A control must improve security while preserving required work. Small, measured changes are easier to troubleshoot than a hundred unexplained changes.
questions.answer: Apply an appropriate baseline, test representative systems, stage changes, schedule deployment where necessary, and verify success with rollback available. Remove unnecessary services and limit privileged access. A firewall can reduce exposure to a vulnerable service, but that does not repair the flaw or eliminate other attack paths. Legacy tools such as EMET, WSUS, or old scanner screenshots illustrate functions, not a requirement to install historical versions. The four discussion factors reduce distribution, coordination, analysis, and testing pressure.
questions.example: Five baseline changes are tested before rollout. A broken business application can then be traced to a small set of candidate changes.
questions.correct: Test staged changes and confirm both security and required functionality
distractors: Blocked traffic proves all flaws are fixed
questions.goal: Explain Controlled hardening and patch validation in your own words, recognize a concrete example, and justify the matching protection or limitation.
questions.pitfall: Apply every change without records

questions.title: NAC policy and endpoint controls
questions.q: How do NAC, GPO, endpoint firewall, and HIPS contribute different protections?
questions.teach: NAC decides whether a device meets conditions for access. GPO distributes settings. Endpoint firewall and HIPS enforce or observe activity on a host.
questions.answer: Lecture 5 uses a traveling workstation to explain posture checks: patch status, antivirus definitions, and required policies can influence access. GPO helps distribute Windows-domain policy settings. An endpoint firewall restricts network communication to host services, while HIPS can respond to selected local behaviors or patterns. None eliminates the need to verify actual configuration, investigate alerts, or protect accounts. A domain user can still have excessive rights if configured incorrectly.
questions.example: A returning laptop is checked before receiving normal access. Its required firewall policy must also be present and effective after connection.
questions.correct: Access posture, configuration distribution, and local enforcement complement each other
distractors: GPO automatically authenticates every external site
A domain account can never be privileged
questions.goal: Explain NAC policy and endpoint controls in your own words, recognize a concrete example, and justify the matching protection or limitation.
questions.pitfall: GPO automatically authenticates every external site

questions.title: Manual automated static and dynamic
questions.q: Why are these four analysis labels not interchangeable?
questions.teach: Manual versus automated asks who performs the work. Static versus dynamic asks whether the code being analyzed runs.
questions.answer: A person can read source statically or debug running code dynamically. A tool can automate either approach. Lecture 6 names Firebug and Malzilla for manual review and JSUnpack, Wepawet, and reputation services under automated tools. Inspect source for suspicious redirects, embedded frames, scripts, form handling, and external references. Legitimate pages can contain those features too, so context and behavior matter. JSUnpack is the likely sample answer but the slide’s actual category is automated, not a definitive purely-static classification.
questions.example: A script automatically scans source without executing it: automated/static. A human watches an isolated program’s network changes: manual/dynamic.
questions.correct: Manual/automated and static/dynamic describe two independent dimensions
questions.goal: Explain Manual automated static and dynamic in your own words, recognize a concrete example, and justify the matching protection or limitation.
questions.pitfall: All automated analysis is static

questions.title: Reputation and behavior evidence
questions.q: Why can two website scanners disagree, and why does time matter?
questions.teach: A site can change after its last scan. A reputation label summarizes previous observations, not every possible current response.
questions.answer: Reputation services rely on their scan history, reporting, and classification. A newly compromised legitimate page may not yet be listed. Different user agents, times, or visitor conditions may receive different content. Dynamic inspection observes files, registry, processes, and connections in a controlled environment; a negative result may reflect the test conditions. Isolation reduces risk but is not an absolute guarantee. Do not browse historical malicious domains from lecture screenshots as study exercises.
questions.example: One service reports an old clean scan, while a sandbox sees a new redirect only for a particular browser. The evidence needs reconciliation, not blind voting.
questions.correct: Compare observation time, test conditions, and the evidence behind each result
distractors: A recognizable URL guarantees safety forever
One clean reputation score proves no compromise
A VM can never affect its host
questions.goal: Explain Reputation and behavior evidence in your own words, recognize a concrete example, and justify the matching protection or limitation.
questions.pitfall: A recognizable URL guarantees safety forever

questions.title: Merkle proofs and hash links
questions.q: How does a Merkle proof differ from a link to the previous block?
questions.teach: One commitment summarizes transactions inside a block. Another connects that block to earlier history.
questions.answer: A Merkle tree combines transaction hashes into a root. A membership proof supplies enough sibling hashes to recompute the trusted root without downloading every transaction. It shows inclusion under that root, not that a real-world claim is true or a spend valid. A previous-block hash commits to the preceding header. Non-membership proofs require appropriate ordered/authenticated structures; not every ordinary Merkle tree automatically proves absence. Changing data affects its commitment and descendant links.
questions.example: A lightweight client can verify inclusion using a transaction and its proof path, but still needs an appropriately trusted chain/header view and validation assumptions.
questions.correct: Merkle proofs show inclusion under a root; prior hashes link block history
distractors: A Merkle proof reveals every owner’s private key
Membership proves every business claim is true
Any unsorted tree automatically proves absence
questions.goal: Explain Merkle proofs and hash links in your own words, recognize a concrete example, and justify the matching protection or limitation.
questions.pitfall: A Merkle proof reveals every owner’s private key

questions.title: Consensus double spending and forks
questions.q: Why do valid signatures alone not solve the double-spending problem?
questions.teach: The same owner might authorize two conflicting spends. The network needs rules and agreement about which valid history to accept.
questions.answer: Nodes independently validate transactions and blocks. Bitcoin’s proof-of-work chain selection follows greatest cumulative work among valid chains; the lecture’s longest-chain phrase is a simplification. The Byzantine-generals theme concerns agreement despite faulty or malicious participants. Confirmations reduce reorganization risk under the security assumptions. A hard fork changes rules incompatibly; a soft fork restricts accepted rules compatibly for older nodes. Neither term simply means every competing branch survives or disappears by natural selection.
questions.example: Two transactions spend the same previous output and both have genuine owner signatures. They cannot both enter the same valid transaction history.
questions.correct: Validation and consensus choose a valid history among conflicting possibilities
distractors: A valid signature makes every conflicting spend acceptable
Any chain with more block count is always valid
Every hard fork guarantees two permanent chains
refs: security challenges chain selection and forks
questions.goal: Explain Consensus double spending and forks in your own words, recognize a concrete example, and justify the matching protection or limitation.
questions.pitfall: A valid signature makes every conflicting spend acceptable

questions.title: Packets encapsulation and headers
questions.q: How do application data, TCP segments, and IP packets fit together?
questions.teach: Picture nested envelopes. Each layer adds information for its own job; the whole packet is not just the user’s message.
questions.answer: Application data can be carried in a TCP segment with ports, sequence/acknowledgment fields, and a checksum. IP wraps transport data with addresses and routing-related header fields. A link-layer frame carries the IP packet on a particular link. Packet lengths vary within protocol/link constraints. TCP is transport/OSI layer 4; IP is network/OSI layer 3. TCP does not choose the Internet route or provide encryption. Checksum error detection is distinct from authenticated integrity.
questions.example: A short message gains TCP and IP headers before link transmission. A capture can show ports and addresses even when higher-level contents are encrypted.
questions.correct: Transport data is encapsulated inside IP, then a link frame
distractors: TCP contains the entire Internet routing table
Every IP packet has the same fixed size
questions.goal: Explain Packets encapsulation and headers in your own words, recognize a concrete example, and justify the matching protection or limitation.
questions.pitfall: TCP contains the entire Internet routing table

questions.title: Firewall types and return-traffic assumptions
questions.q: How do packet filtering, circuit gateways, and application gateways differ?
questions.teach: Different controls see different details. A port or flag alone does not prove a request belongs to a permitted conversation.
questions.answer: The lecture diagram associates packet filtering with network-level checks, circuit gateways with connection/session establishment, application gateways with higher-level mediation, and MAC-layer controls with link identifiers. Modern products may combine capabilities. Stateful filtering tracks connection context; a simplistic rule allowing anything resembling return traffic can be misleading. A proxy may authenticate users and restrict requests, but its visibility and policies determine effectiveness. Compare business goals and inspectable evidence rather than assuming one name guarantees protection.
questions.example: A network rule sees an IP and port; an application proxy can apply a website-category policy. Neither replaces endpoint evidence about which process initiated a connection.
questions.correct: Inspect information available at the relevant layer and connection context
distractors: Every allowed ACK proves an established session
A proxy always defeats every reverse shell
MAC filtering verifies a person’s identity
questions.goal: Explain Firewall types and return-traffic assumptions in your own words, recognize a concrete example, and justify the matching protection or limitation.
questions.pitfall: Every allowed ACK proves an established session

questions.title: Secure protocol choices
questions.q: How do FTP, FTPS, SFTP, HTTPS, S/MIME, SRTP, and NTP differ?
questions.teach: Similar names can hide different protocols. Choose the protection and application first.
questions.answer: Traditional FTP uses separate control/data connections without encryption. FTPS adds TLS to FTP; require the intended protection for control and data rather than assuming both are protected. SFTP is file transfer over SSH, not FTP with a secure label. HTTPS protects HTTP with TLS. S/MIME supports email content signing/encryption, subject to key and client support. SRTP protects real-time media. NTP synchronizes time; plain NTP alone is not a cryptographic guarantee (NTS is a separate security mechanism). DNSSEC authenticates DNS data and does not encrypt ordinary queries. These clarify the lecture’s simplified secure-protocol table.
questions.example: A company moving files chooses SFTP over SSH. A signed email may remain signed beyond one transport connection, unlike merely protecting its delivery link with TLS.
questions.correct: Match the application and verify the actual security mechanism
refs: secure file transfer email and protocol table
questions.goal: Explain Secure protocol choices in your own words, recognize a concrete example, and justify the matching protection or limitation.
questions.pitfall: SFTP and FTPS are identical

questions.title: DNS SNMP and diagnostic evidence
questions.q: What can DNS, SNMP, and ICMP tell an administrator?
questions.teach: Naming, management statistics, and reachability are different questions. A single successful diagnostic does not prove the whole service is healthy.
questions.answer: DNS provides hierarchical distributed name records. Poisoning can redirect resolution; validated DNSSEC checks signed DNS data. Restricting unintended zone transfer reduces information exposure. SNMP agents expose permitted management information; versions 1/2c use community strings, while v3 supports stronger authentication/privacy depending on configuration. ICMP echo can test reachability and latency, but a blocked response does not prove the host is down. A successful ping does not prove that an application works.
questions.example: A device answers ping but its web application fails. The network evidence establishes only part of the service path, so application logs and connection tests are needed.
questions.correct: Use each protocol’s evidence for the question it can answer
distractors: A successful ping proves every application is healthy
SNMP community strings always encrypt traffic
DNSSEC makes all returned websites trustworthy
questions.goal: Explain DNS SNMP and diagnostic evidence in your own words, recognize a concrete example, and justify the matching protection or limitation.
questions.pitfall: A successful ping proves every application is healthy

questions.title: Port mirrors taps and sensor placement
questions.q: Why does sensor placement determine what defenders can see?
questions.teach: A sensor cannot inspect traffic it never receives. Define the visibility question before selecting its network location.
questions.answer: A switch mirror copies selected port traffic to a monitoring port. A network tap provides a traffic copy from a link. Both have operational limitations; traffic may be dropped, selected incompletely, or remain encrypted. Sensors detect, collectors gather, filters enforce, and correlation engines combine evidence. Placement should cover relevant boundaries, internal movement, and business assets; simply choosing the busiest link can miss a smaller critical segment. TLS termination changes which content may be visible.
questions.example: A gateway sensor sees Internet traffic but not two servers talking locally on another switch. An internal mirror or other telemetry may be needed.
questions.correct: Place sensors where the required traffic is observable and correlate other evidence
distractors: The busiest link reveals every network action
A collector always blocks malware inline
questions.goal: Explain Port mirrors taps and sensor placement in your own words, recognize a concrete example, and justify the matching protection or limitation.
questions.pitfall: The busiest link reveals every network action

questions.title: Logs correlation and retention
questions.q: How do access audit event and security logs support an investigation?
questions.teach: Each log is a partial witness. Put the witnesses on a common timeline and preserve the evidence needed to explain what happened.
questions.answer: Access logs show resource requests, audit logs record accountable actions, event logs record system/application events, and security logs describe security-related observations. Exact fields vary. Correlate identity, host, and network events using reliable time and context. Watch rejected traffic, unusual outbound connections, unsuccessful logins, and unexpected file changes. Centralized analysis helps handle volume and format differences, but collection gaps, clock differences, retention limits, and tampering affect conclusions. File-integrity monitoring detects changes; an alert still needs interpretation.
questions.example: An unusual login precedes a new process and outbound transfer. Together these support a stronger timeline than any one record alone.
questions.correct: Correlate partial records while checking time, coverage, integrity, and retention
distractors: One log contains every action forever
No retained event proves nothing happened
All file changes are definitely malicious
refs: analyzing security data and log management
questions.goal: Explain Logs correlation and retention in your own words, recognize a concrete example, and justify the matching protection or limitation.
questions.pitfall: One log contains every action forever

questions.title: Hypervisors containers and virtual desktops
questions.q: How do Type I Type II containers VDI and VM sprawl differ?
questions.teach: A VM has a guest operating system. A container usually shares the host kernel. A virtual desktop describes where a user’s desktop runs.
questions.answer: Type I hypervisors run directly on hardware; Type II hypervisors run above a host OS, as in the VirtualBox lab. Containers package applications and dependencies while sharing a kernel, with different isolation boundaries from VMs. VDI hosts user desktops on servers. Snapshots and live migration support operations but do not automatically remove downtime or replace backups. VM escape is a possible isolation failure; VM sprawl is unmanaged growth. Protect the hypervisor, guests, management plane, and virtual networks. Virtual Distributed Ethernet (VDE) describes a virtual Ethernet network connecting virtual and/or physical systems; it is a networking concept, distinct from VDI’s remotely hosted desktops.
questions.example: An organization creates twenty test VMs and forgets half of them. Those systems still need ownership, updates, and monitoring.
questions.correct: Distinguish the OS and management boundaries of each model
distractors: Every container has its own full guest kernel
A snapshot is an independent backup by definition
questions.goal: Explain Hypervisors containers and virtual desktops in your own words, recognize a concrete example, and justify the matching protection or limitation.
questions.pitfall: Every container has its own full guest kernel

questions.title: Cloud models and responsibility
questions.q: How do SaaS PaaS IaaS and cloud deployment models affect security duties?
questions.teach: The provider manages some layers and the customer manages others. Renting infrastructure does not transfer every security decision.
questions.answer: SaaS supplies an application; PaaS supplies a managed platform for customer applications; IaaS supplies infrastructure where customers manage their OS/applications. SECaaS delivers security services. Public/private/community/hybrid describe deployment arrangements, not the same categories as service models. Protect identities, configurations, data, transmission, tenant isolation, and availability according to responsibility. A CASB helps extend enterprise policy to cloud usage. Distributed processing does not by itself mean every participant has equal authority. A public cloud offers provider services to customers generally; a private cloud is dedicated to one organization; a community cloud serves organizations with shared needs; a hybrid combines distinct cloud arrangements with integration. These describe deployment, while SaaS/PaaS/IaaS describe which service layers are supplied.
questions.example: An IaaS customer still patches its own guest OS. A SaaS customer may not patch the vendor’s servers but still controls its own user access and data-sharing choices.
questions.correct: Allocate duties by service model and verify the actual shared-responsibility boundary
distractors: Cloud always means the provider patches every customer OS
Private cloud means there is no network
SaaS and hybrid are the same kind of category
questions.goal: Explain Cloud models and responsibility in your own words, recognize a concrete example, and justify the matching protection or limitation.
questions.pitfall: Cloud always means the provider patches every customer OS

checks.q: A payroll file is encrypted before transfer. Someone who intercepts the file sees ciphertext and needs the appropriate decryption key to read it. Which principle explains this?
checks.correct: True
checks.teach: Plaintext is the readable message. Ciphertext is its encrypted representation. A digest is a different kind of output.
checks.answer: TRUE. Encryption transforms plaintext into ciphertext using an algorithm and key. Decryption recovers plaintext using the appropriate key. Hashing instead produces a digest for comparison and has no decryption operation.
checks.example: A payroll file is encrypted before transfer. Someone who intercepts the file sees ciphertext and needs the appropriate decryption key to read it.

checks.q: An attacker steals a student’s login and recovery information, then uses the account to impersonate the student or access additional services. Which principle explains this?
checks.correct: True
checks.teach: Data can have value because it helps impersonate a person or reach another account. Payment details are only one target.
checks.answer: TRUE. Personal information, credentials, health records, private communications, and intellectual property can support fraud, extortion, resale, and espionage. The textbook’s social-engineering example shows why account-recovery information can be valuable even without a full card number.
checks.example: An attacker steals a student’s login and recovery information, then uses the account to impersonate the student or access additional services.

checks.q: A mail application resolves a server name with DNS, connects using transport protocols, and uses SMTP to send mail. Several suite members cooperate. Which principle explains this?
checks.correct: True
checks.teach: The suite is the whole family. TCP and IP are central members with different jobs.
checks.answer: TRUE with a spelling correction: SMTP, not SMPT. TCP/IP names a protocol suite spanning layers. DNS resolves names, SNMP supports device management, SMTP transfers mail, POP retrieves mail, and FTP transfers files. They are not all transport-layer protocols.
checks.example: A mail application resolves a server name with DNS, connects using transport protocols, and uses SMTP to send mail. Several suite members cooperate.

checks.q: An employee evaluates staff security needs and designs a suitable access-control solution while managing daily security technology. That matches the administrator role in the book. Which principle explains this?
checks.correct: Security administrator
checks.teach: Match the duties to this textbook’s definition. Job titles at actual companies can vary.
checks.answer: A. Security administrator. Ciampa Chapter 1, printed page 6 (PDF page 34), assigns these duties to the security administrator. A technician configures and troubleshoots tools; a manager supervises personnel; the CISO directs security at the executive level. This resolves the second guide’s textbook-needed placeholder.
checks.example: An employee evaluates staff security needs and designs a suitable access-control solution while managing daily security technology. That matches the administrator role in the book.

checks.q: Two checkout requests both see one remaining item before either updates stock. Both complete, selling the same item twice. Which principle explains this?
checks.correct: Concurrent execution accesses a shared resource and causes unintended consequences
distractors: A race to patch a newly discovered vulnerability
A software update released before discovery
An attack finishing before antivirus scanning
checks.teach: Two operations interfere because each assumes it can use the same state safely. Locking, atomic operations, or safe transaction design can prevent this.
checks.answer: D. Concurrent execution accesses shared state without adequate synchronization, so the result depends on timing or ordering and can become unintended. A race condition is a concurrency flaw, not a synonym for DDoS, slow processing, or a race to patch before attackers act.
checks.example: Two checkout requests both see one remaining item before either updates stock. Both complete, selling the same item twice.

checks.q: A caller claims to be the help desk and asks for a login code. Hang up and verify through an independently known help-desk number. Which principle explains this?
checks.correct: VoIP makes caller-ID spoofing easier
distractors: It is only tailored to organizations
It always uses a real person to call
checks.teach: Voice is the identifying feature. Caller ID is a claim, not proof of identity.
checks.answer: C. VoIP makes caller-ID spoofing easier. Vishing is voice phishing: an attacker uses a call or voice message to trick someone into revealing information or performing an action. Calls can be automated, targeted, or broadly distributed; it does not always require a live person.
checks.example: A caller claims to be the help desk and asks for a login code. Hang up and verify through an independently known help-desk number.

checks.q: An email claims to come from campus IT but uses a lookalike domain and urgent password language. Preserve the message and inspect headers through the approved reporting process. Which principle explains this?
checks.correct: Email header
checks.teach: Headers provide evidence for investigation. Reading the visible sender label alone is not enough.
checks.answer: D. Email header. Full headers provide routing and sender-related fields such as Received, Return-Path, and authentication results. Compare these with the claimed sender and timestamps. A display name, body, attachment, or embedded URL alone does not establish who sent the message. Some header fields can also be forged; establish trusted receiving-system boundaries.
checks.example: An email claims to come from campus IT but uses a lookalike domain and urgent password language. Preserve the message and inspect headers through the approved reporting process.

checks.q: A file download needs all bytes in order. TCP can retransmit missing data; TLS is needed separately to protect confidentiality and authenticate the server. Which principle explains this?
checks.correct: TCP
checks.teach: TCP handles reliable delivery. It does not itself encrypt your message or prove the other party’s identity.
checks.answer: A. TCP is the likely intended answer: Transmission Control Protocol provides reliable, ordered byte-stream delivery using acknowledgments, retransmissions, sequencing, and a checksum. IP supplies addressing and routing. TCP’s reliability and checksum are not confidentiality or cryptographic authentication. HTTPS adds TLS security at a different level. The phrase basic security in the prompt is loose.
checks.example: A file download needs all bytes in order. TCP can retransmit missing data; TLS is needed separately to protect confidentiality and authenticate the server.

checks.q: A legitimate backup triggers a malware alert: false positive. A real malicious download produces no alert: false negative. Which principle explains this?
checks.correct: False positive
checks.teach: Positive means the system says threat. False means that conclusion is wrong.
checks.answer: False positive, also called a Type I error in your notes. A false negative (Type II) occurs when malicious traffic is treated as benign. False positives consume analyst time and can interrupt legitimate work if prevention blocks the traffic; false negatives leave attacks undetected.
checks.example: A legitimate backup triggers a malware alert: false positive. A real malicious download produces no alert: false negative.

checks.q: One group adopts a rule that older nodes reject while another group continues the old rules. Their accepted transaction histories can diverge. Which principle explains this?
checks.correct: Hard fork
checks.teach: A protocol disagreement is different from two miners briefly finding competing blocks.
checks.answer: Hard fork is the guide’s intended term. It changes consensus rules incompatibly, so nodes following different rules can maintain different chains. A persistent split depends on participants continuing both histories; a hard fork need not always leave two lasting communities. A soft fork tightens accepted rules compatibly for older nodes.
checks.example: One group adopts a rule that older nodes reject while another group continues the old rules. Their accepted transaction histories can diverge.

checks.q: A bit flips while a segment is transmitted and the checksum comparison fails. The receiver can discard it; reliable transport may retransmit. Which principle explains this?
checks.correct: Checksum
checks.teach: An error check catches transmission damage. Authenticating malicious changes requires a stronger, trusted construction.
checks.answer: Checksum. The receiver recomputes an error-detection value and compares it with the transmitted value to detect accidental corruption. An ordinary Internet checksum is not SHA-256 and does not defend against an attacker who can alter data and recompute the checksum. Cryptographic integrity requires a suitable authenticated mechanism such as a MAC or signature.
checks.example: A bit flips while a segment is transmitted and the checksum comparison fails. The receiver can discard it; reliable transport may retransmit.

checks.q: A business inventories vulnerable devices, prioritizes exposed servers, tests a patch on representative VMs, pilots deployment, monitors failures, and rolls out in stages with rollback available. Which principle explains this?
checks.correct: Distribution, coordination, prioritization, and safe testing become easier
distractors: All updates can be installed without testing
Snapshots eliminate the need for backups
Cloud providers automatically patch every customer application
checks.teach: Organize your discussion by the bottleneck each technology reduces. State one benefit and one limitation for each.
checks.answer: More bandwidth speeds patch distribution, although deployments still need scheduling. Cloud-based and centralized management can coordinate updates across fleets, while customers retain responsibilities for their own systems and configurations. Analytics helps inventory systems, prioritize exposure, and detect failed updates. Virtualization supports representative test environments, snapshots, and rollback. Together these reduce transfer, coordination, decision, and testing costs. They do not remove compatibility testing, outages, or zero-day risk.
checks.example: A business inventories vulnerable devices, prioritizes exposed servers, tests a patch on representative VMs, pilots deployment, monitors failures, and rolls out in stages with rollback available.

checks.q: An infected document executes a malicious macro; a network worm spreads independently; a fake antivirus page scares a user into paying. Each has a different mechanism and defense. Which principle explains this?
checks.correct: Virus needs a host; worm propagates independently; other names describe behavior
distractors: Backdoors are the same as checksums
checks.teach: Compare how malware spreads, hides, and acts. These categories can overlap: a backdoor may install spyware that includes a keylogger.
checks.answer: A virus attaches to a host file or document and replicates when the host runs; a worm is a standalone program that can propagate across networks. Scareware uses fraudulent alarms to pressure payment or installation. Adware displays unwanted advertising; spyware secretly collects information; a backdoor bypasses normal access controls. In this textbook’s Chapter 2, viruses include program/file viruses and macro viruses, with appender infection and armored concealment techniques: Swiss cheese, split infection, oligomorphic, polymorphic, and metamorphic mutation. Boot-sector viruses are another common category, but the supplied edition emphasizes the preceding list. The guide labels this Ch. 1; the relevant detail is actually Ch. 2, pp. 55–65.
checks.example: An infected document executes a malicious macro; a network worm spreads independently; a fake antivirus page scares a user into paying. Each has a different mechanism and defense.

checks.q: A sender signs a document with the sender’s private signing key and protects the content for the recipient. The recipient decrypts and verifies using the appropriate keys and a trusted identity binding. Which principle explains this?
checks.correct: Encryption protects reading; authentication proves origin; obfuscation obscures details
distractors: A hash alone proves the sender
A signature automatically hides the message
checks.teach: Ask three separate questions: who can read, who created or approved it, and what details are being obscured?
checks.answer: Confidentiality limits who can read data, usually through encryption. Authentication establishes a claimed identity or data origin through a suitable cryptographic protocol; a digital signature can bind a message to a signing key. Obfuscation makes information or implementation details harder to understand, and the textbook includes it among cryptographic protections. These goals complement one another but do not substitute for one another. Encryption to a recipient’s public key does not by itself identify the sender; an ordinary hash does not authenticate an origin; signing does not encrypt the message. For secrecy plus sender authentication, use a properly designed encrypted and authenticated scheme.
checks.example: A sender signs a document with the sender’s private signing key and protects the content for the recipient. The recipient decrypts and verifies using the appropriate keys and a trusted identity binding.

checks.q: Two distinct files could share a digest. A trusted expected hash can help verify a download, but an attacker changing both file and untrusted posted hash defeats that simple comparison. Which principle explains this?
checks.correct: Large well-distributed outputs make finding collisions computationally difficult
distractors: All hash algorithms have equal collision resistance
checks.teach: A large output space makes a matching pair hard to find, but fixed-length outputs cannot uniquely represent every possible input.
checks.answer: Qualify the premise: a well-designed cryptographic hash aims for computational collision resistance. A fixed n-bit digest has 2^n possible outputs, so different inputs must sometimes collide. Good output distribution and no practical structural shortcuts make finding a collision expensive. The generic birthday bound is roughly 2^(n/2) work to find any pair; finding an input for a particular digest is a different preimage problem. SHA-256 produces 256 bits (64 hexadecimal characters), with an ideal generic collision bound around 2^128. MD5 and SHA-1 demonstrate that not every hash is collision resistant. Collision resistant never means collision impossible.
checks.example: Two distinct files could share a digest. A trusted expected hash can help verify a download, but an attacker changing both file and untrusted posted hash defeats that simple comparison.

checks.q: Change an old record in a teaching chain. Its hash and descendants no longer match. Rehashing a local copy is easy in a toy demo; convincing a real consensus network is the costly part. Which principle explains this?
checks.correct: Hash links plus validation and consensus create a shared tamper-evident history
distractors: Encryption alone makes every transaction private
A nonce is the owner’s password
Every blockchain must use Bitcoin mining
checks.teach: Hashes connect history; signatures authorize spending; consensus resolves competing histories. None does all three jobs alone.
checks.answer: Transactions are grouped into blocks. A block header commits to transaction data through a Merkle root and includes the previous block’s hash. Altering data changes its hash and breaks later commitments. Nodes validate transactions and consensus determines the accepted history. In Bitcoin, proof of work requires miners to search nonces for a header hash meeting a target; the accepted valid chain has the greatest cumulative work. More confirmations make rewriting history harder under the network’s security assumptions. Benefits include shared auditability and tamper evidence. Costs include proof-of-work energy use, throughput/latency limits, public-data privacy issues, key loss, and difficult correction of erroneous entries. Blockchain is not an absolute guarantee of truth or immutability, and not all blockchains use proof of work.
checks.example: Change an old record in a teaching chain. Its hash and descendants no longer match. Rehashing a local copy is easy in a toy demo; convincing a real consensus network is the costly part.

checks.q: Alice signs a transaction spending an output she controls and creating one for Bob. Others verify it with public information. Bob later spends by satisfying his output’s conditions. Which principle explains this?
checks.correct: A peer-to-peer currency with signature-authorized spending and blockchain consensus
distractors: A coin encrypted with SHA-256 and emailed
A central-bank database with no signatures
An anonymous password shared by all miners
checks.teach: Ownership means the ability to authorize spending under the output’s rules. You transfer spending rights through a transaction; you do not email a secret coin file.
checks.answer: Bitcoin is a peer-to-peer digital currency whose transaction history is recorded on a blockchain. A spender authorizes use of earlier unspent transaction outputs by satisfying their spending conditions, typically with a digital signature created using the spender’s private key. A new output specifies conditions for the receiver. Nodes verify authorization and check for double spending; mining orders valid transactions through proof of work. SHA-256 contributes to hashing and proof of work, not encryption of a coin. An address is commonly derived from a key or script and is not always the raw public key. Public ledger transparency provides pseudonymity, not guaranteed anonymity. Miners receive a block subsidy and transaction fees as incentives.
checks.example: Alice signs a transaction spending an output she controls and creating one for Bob. Others verify it with public information. Bob later spends by satisfying his output’s conditions.

checks.q: A hospital considers ransomware risk to patient records. Backups improve recovery, access controls restrict disclosure, and monitoring detects changes. Which principle explains this?
checks.correct: Disclosure, alteration, and loss of access
distractors: The same property under three names
checks.teach: A leaked record harms confidentiality; a changed grade harms integrity; an unavailable portal harms availability.
checks.answer: Confidentiality restricts disclosure, integrity protects against unauthorized alteration, and availability provides access when needed. An asset has value; a vulnerability is a weakness; a threat can cause harm; risk concerns likelihood and impact. Risk responses include accept, avoid, mitigate, and transfer. Controls can be technical, administrative, or physical.
checks.example: A hospital considers ransomware risk to patient records. Backups improve recovery, access controls restrict disclosure, and monitoring detects changes.

checks.q: A disgruntled staff member has access to payroll. An outside criminal uses a phishing toolkit. The controls must account for both trusted and untrusted access. Which principle explains this?
checks.correct: Motivation, capability, resources, and access help assess threats
distractors: Every attacker needs advanced programming skills
checks.teach: Identify who, why, capability, and access rather than assuming one threat always ranks first.
checks.answer: Organized crime often seeks profit; hacktivists pursue ideological goals; nation-state actors may seek espionage or disruption; insiders already have trusted access; script kiddies rely on existing tools; vulnerability brokers sell knowledge. Advanced persistent threats involve sustained, targeted activity. Zero-day describes an unknown or unpatched vulnerability context, not a person. Your notes emphasize social engineering and insiders as pressing concerns; actual priority depends on organizational exposure.
checks.example: A disgruntled staff member has access to payroll. An outside criminal uses a phishing toolkit. The controls must account for both trusted and untrusted access.

checks.q: Email filtering, a standard-user account, endpoint monitoring, and recovery procedures protect different points in a phishing incident. Which principle explains this?
checks.correct: Layer controls, limit rights, diversify, obscure details, and keep management simple
distractors: Publish all secrets to simplify access
checks.teach: Several well-managed controls help more than one opaque, overcomplicated control.
checks.answer: Layering adds multiple safeguards. Limiting gives only necessary access. Diversity reduces shared failure modes across products or controls. Obscurity hides unnecessary details but cannot be the sole defense. Simplicity makes controls easier to understand and manage. Frameworks and reference architectures organize a security program; some are regulatory, industry-specific, national, or international.
checks.example: Email filtering, a standard-user account, endpoint monitoring, and recovery procedures protect different points in a phishing incident.

checks.q: A retailer inspects gateway traffic, segments payment systems, collects endpoint events, and uses redundant devices to avoid a single outage. Which principle explains this?
checks.correct: Layered inspection and telemetry with capacity and availability planning
distractors: A perimeter firewall eliminates all endpoint risk
Visibility means capturing only public web pages
checks.teach: A strong front door cannot show what is happening inside every room. Host and internal telemetry fill that gap.
checks.answer: Use safeguards at both perimeter and endpoint. A choke point is a controlled entry or exit where traffic can be inspected; internal segmentation also matters. Visibility requires useful telemetry at these boundaries and on hosts. Redundancy reduces single points of failure, while scalability supports changing workload. Balance security with business availability, budget, and capacity.
checks.example: A retailer inspects gateway traffic, segments payment systems, collects endpoint events, and uses redundant devices to avoid a single outage.

checks.q: An alert-only sensor reports suspicious traffic. An inline prevention rule blocks the same traffic, potentially interrupting legitimate service if the rule is wrong. Which principle explains this?
checks.correct: IDS alerts; IPS can actively intervene
distractors: An antivirus database makes false negatives impossible
checks.teach: Detection versus prevention describes the response, not whether the tool possesses its own intelligence.
checks.answer: An IDS detects suspicious activity and alerts. An IPS can actively block or disrupt traffic or activity. Either can use signatures, heuristics, behavior, or other techniques; an IPS does not require AI. Host IPS observes local activity; network controls observe traffic. Tune false positives and false negatives in light of business impact.
checks.example: An alert-only sensor reports suspicious traffic. An inline prevention rule blocks the same traffic, potentially interrupting legitimate service if the rule is wrong.

checks.q: An analyst finds a long outbound connection in flow logs, examines available packet evidence, then correlates it with proxy and endpoint events. Which principle explains this?
checks.correct: PCAP captures bytes; flow summarizes; proxy mediates; allowlisting restricts execution
distractors: Flow records always include every file
A proxy is the same as PCAP
checks.teach: Choose the evidence or control for the question: content, conversation metadata, mediated requests, or permitted programs.
checks.answer: Full PCAP records packet bytes within capture limits, useful for detailed reconstruction; encrypted payloads remain encrypted without suitable keys. Flow records summarize conversations such as endpoints, times, ports, and byte counts. A proxy mediates application requests and can enforce policy and log activity. Application allowlisting permits approved software and restricts other execution. These controls complement rather than replace one another.
checks.example: An analyst finds a long outbound connection in flow logs, examines available packet evidence, then correlates it with proxy and endpoint events.

checks.q: A service is unavailable despite modest bandwidth because many connections remain incomplete. Appropriate connection limits and timeouts address this pattern. Which principle explains this?
checks.correct: They consume connection resources and deny legitimate access
distractors: All DoS attacks require a giant botnet
A SYN flood is simply a race condition
checks.teach: Bandwidth floods and application connection exhaustion stress different resources. Match mitigation to the bottleneck.
checks.answer: Denial of service exhausts resources or disrupts access; distributed DoS uses multiple sources. A SYN flood abuses half-open TCP connection state. Slowloris holds many HTTP connections with incomplete, slow requests and may work from few sources. Mitigations include upstream filtering, rate and connection limits, appropriate timeouts, SYN protections, and capacity planning. DDoS can distract responders but is not always a distraction or a race condition.
checks.example: A service is unavailable despite modest bandwidth because many connections remain incomplete. Appropriate connection limits and timeouts address this pattern.

checks.q: A search value must remain a SQL parameter. A comment displayed on a page must remain text or sanitized allowed HTML rather than executable script. Which principle explains this?
checks.correct: SQLi changes query interpretation; XSS executes script in the browser
distractors: Both are prevented by antivirus alone
XSS always takes full control of the application server
Prepared statements alone prevent every XSS flaw
checks.teach: Ask where the injected content is interpreted: database query engine or victim browser. XSS is not automatically full server control.
checks.answer: SQL injection makes untrusted input influence database query structure. Parameterized queries keep data separate from SQL commands; least-privilege database accounts limit harm. XSS causes attacker-controlled script to execute in a user’s browser in a trusted site’s context. Use context-aware output encoding, safe APIs, and appropriate sanitization for allowed HTML. Input validation supports both but is insufficient alone. WebGoat is a deliberately vulnerable teaching application. Neither attack is limited to one operating system.
checks.example: A search value must remain a SQL parameter. A comment displayed on a page must remain text or sanitized allowed HTML rather than executable script.

checks.q: An urgent campus-password message aimed at named students is targeted phishing. A phone request for login codes is vishing. Which principle explains this?
checks.correct: Targeting and communication channel distinguish the methods
checks.teach: Channel, targeting, and pretext distinguish these related attacks.
checks.answer: Phishing uses deceptive communication to elicit information or action. Spear phishing targets particular recipients using tailored context. Smishing uses SMS; vishing uses voice. A 419 or advance-fee scam promises a benefit to obtain money or sensitive data upfront. Scareware creates false security urgency. Verify requests through independent trusted channels and report suspicious messages.
checks.example: An urgent campus-password message aimed at named students is targeted phishing. A phone request for login codes is vishing.

checks.q: A fake staff login collects a test password in the isolated lab. A business analogue is account takeover leading to exposed records or fraudulent actions. Which principle explains this?
checks.correct: Structured testing and social-engineering simulation reveal technical and human weaknesses
distractors: Patching alone prevents every fake-login attack
A captured password always means code executed on the host
checks.teach: Explain the weakness, business consequence, evidence, and defense. Exact tool-menu commands are not the stated exam priority.
checks.answer: Metasploit organizes authorized security testing through exploit, payload, auxiliary, and post-exploitation capabilities. SET is a separate TrustedSec social-engineering toolkit that can integrate with Metasploit; it is not simply a Metasploit module. The credential-harvesting lab demonstrates how user trust can disclose credentials without a software exploit. Prevent with training, filtering, phishing-resistant MFA, and login monitoring. If credentials are disclosed, report, reset affected secrets from a trusted device, revoke sessions, and investigate related access.
checks.example: A fake staff login collects a test password in the isolated lab. A business analogue is account takeover leading to exposed records or fraudulent actions.

checks.q: The lab’s isolated victim records test keystrokes. An organization should investigate the endpoint and account access rather than assume HTTPS prevented disclosure. Which principle explains this?
checks.correct: The endpoint can capture keystrokes before transport encryption
distractors: Only encrypted keystrokes can be logged
checks.teach: Protection during transmission does not protect the moment data is typed on a compromised device.
checks.answer: A keylogger records input on the endpoint, often before TLS encrypts it for transport. Software variants may intercept input APIs, run with elevated privileges, or observe forms; hardware variants can sit between keyboard and computer. Not every keylogger requires process injection or admin rights. Defend with endpoint monitoring, least privilege, updates, application controls, physical inspection where appropriate, and phishing-resistant authentication. Transport encryption alone cannot secure a compromised endpoint.
checks.example: The lab’s isolated victim records test keystrokes. An organization should investigate the endpoint and account access rather than assume HTTPS prevented disclosure.

checks.q: A business tests a browser update in a representative VM, deploys to a pilot group, monitors compatibility, then expands rollout. Which principle explains this?
checks.correct: Test updates, reduce services and privileges, enforce controls, and verify
distractors: Disable all production firewalls to match a lab
Allow daily work with administrator rights
Assume automatic updates can never fail
checks.teach: Reduce attack surface and limit damage before an incident. Verify that deployed controls actually work.
checks.answer: Inventory assets, apply tested updates, use standard-user accounts, remove unnecessary services, enable appropriate endpoint firewall and protection, restrict software execution, and monitor changes. A patch workflow downloads, tests, pilots, schedules, deploys, and verifies, with rollback planning. NAC checks access posture; GPO distributes domain policy. Patching addresses known vulnerabilities but does not eliminate zero-days. Legacy tool names in notes are historical examples, not a current shopping list.
checks.example: A business tests a browser update in a representative VM, deploys to a pilot group, monitors compatibility, then expands rollout.

checks.q: An Office process starts unusual PowerShell, followed by a new outbound connection and credential access. Build a timeline, identify affected hosts, preserve evidence, and contain according to the incident plan. Which principle explains this?
checks.correct: Correlate process, network, identity, and file evidence into a timeline
distractors: Treat all PowerShell use as proof of compromise
Sandbox means the same as PowerShell
Exfiltration means installing a software update
checks.teach: Separate the tools, techniques, evidence, and outcomes. Seeing a tool name alone does not establish malicious intent.
checks.answer: Correlate host process events, network connections, authentication logs, and file changes. A SOC coordinates monitoring and response. EDR supplies endpoint detection and response evidence. Reconnaissance gathers information; privilege escalation increases rights; credential dumping extracts stored authentication material; SMB commonly supports network file sharing. Process hollowing replaces or maps malicious code into another process context. PowerShell is an administration shell and scripting environment; a sandbox is an isolated execution environment. DLL means Dynamic Link Library. Infiltration gains entry; exfiltration removes information.
checks.example: An Office process starts unusual PowerShell, followed by a new outbound connection and credential access. Build a timeline, identify affected hosts, preserve evidence, and contain according to the incident plan.

checks.q: A tester uses an isolated guest network to observe activity, takes a baseline snapshot, and restores the guest after the exercise. Which principle explains this?
checks.correct: Isolation and reproducible guest states support controlled testing
distractors: NAT and internal network are identical
Disabling production firewalls is a hardening step
checks.teach: Explain why a control is disabled in a demonstration and why a real organization would enforce it.
checks.answer: The host runs VirtualBox and the guest operating systems. The lab uses Kali and Windows 7 guests with an internal network for guest-to-guest tests and NAT for controlled Internet access during setup. Internal networking does not make the entire host immune; additional adapters and sharing features affect exposure. Static guest addresses support predictable connectivity. Snapshots help restore a known lab state but do not replace independent backups. Disabling a guest firewall was an intentionally weakened lab condition, not a production hardening practice.
checks.example: A tester uses an isolated guest network to observe activity, takes a baseline snapshot, and restores the guest after the exercise.

checks.q: A site’s source includes a hidden redirect. An analyst reviews it, consults reputation evidence, and examines behavior in an approved sandbox. Which principle explains this?
checks.correct: Combine source inspection, isolated behavior observation, and reputation evidence
distractors: A familiar brand proves a page is safe
A clean reputation scan proves no new malware exists
checks.teach: A known domain and a clean reputation report are evidence, not guarantees.
checks.answer: Static work inspects HTML, scripts, redirects, and embedded references without execution. Dynamic work observes behavior in an isolated environment, including processes, files, registry, and traffic. Reputation checks compare against previous reports. Automation is fast but can miss new threats; manual investigation provides context but takes skill and time. A legitimate site can be compromised. Firebug, Malzilla, Wepawet, JSUnpack, SiteAdvisor, and Safe Web are course-era examples.
checks.example: A site’s source includes a hidden redirect. An analyst reviews it, consults reputation evidence, and examines behavior in an approved sandbox.

checks.q: A document can be hashed for comparison, signed to show approval, and encrypted for its intended reader. These operations have separate roles. Which principle explains this?
checks.correct: Encrypt for secrecy, hash for comparison, sign for verifiable authorization
distractors: Decrypt SHA-256 to recover the message
Use a bare hash to prove sender identity
Signing automatically encrypts the whole document
checks.teach: Choose the operation by the required property rather than calling every cryptographic output ciphertext.
checks.answer: Encryption protects content confidentiality and is reversible with the correct key. Hashing produces a deterministic fixed-length digest with no intended inverse. A signature uses a private signing key and is checked with a corresponding public key to authenticate authorized data and detect alteration. A bare hash has no secret and does not prove origin. HMAC combines a secret key and hash for integrity and shared-key authentication; it is not encryption and does not provide the same public verification as a signature.
checks.example: A document can be hashed for comparison, signed to show approval, and encrypted for its intended reader. These operations have separate roles.

checks.q: Alice wants only Bob to read a message and wants Bob to verify her approval. She protects it for Bob and signs it using her own signing key. Which principle explains this?
checks.correct: Recipient keys protect reading; sender keys provide signature verification
distractors: Encrypt with sender public key for only Bob to read
Share all private keys for authentication
Use receiver private key on the sender’s machine
checks.teach: For secrecy think recipient; for signature think sender. Protect private and shared secret keys.
checks.answer: Symmetric encryption shares one secret for encryption and decryption and is efficient for bulk data. Public-key encryption uses the recipient’s public key and recipient’s private key to decrypt. Signing uses the sender’s private key and verification uses the sender’s public key. Verify the binding between a public key and a claimed identity. AES is symmetric; RSA and ECC belong to asymmetric families. DES and 3DES are historical course examples, not preferred new-system choices.
checks.example: Alice wants only Bob to read a message and wants Bob to verify her approval. She protects it for Bob and signs it using her own signing key.

checks.q: 3×27=81 leaves remainder 1 modulo 40. Then 7³ mod 55=13 and 13²⁷ mod 55=7. Which principle explains this?
checks.correct: Choose e coprime to φ(n), then d as its modular inverse
distractors: Use addition instead of modular exponentiation
Make d public and hide e
checks.teach: The private exponent reverses the public exponent modulo n for correctly constructed RSA. Real implementations require safe key sizes and padding.
checks.answer: For distinct primes p and q, n=pq and φ(n)=(p−1)(q−1). Choose e with gcd(e,φ(n))=1 and choose d so ed ≡ 1 mod φ(n). Textbook notation may use m for φ(n). Classroom encryption is c=m^e mod n and decryption is m=c^d mod n. With p=5, q=11, n=55, φ=40, e=3, d=27: message 7 gives ciphertext 13 and decrypts to 7. The notes’ condition using e and n is incorrect; coprimality with φ(n) is essential. Small unpadded examples teach arithmetic and are not secure deployments.
checks.example: 3×27=81 leaves remainder 1 modulo 40. Then 7³ mod 55=13 and 13²⁷ mod 55=7.

checks.q: Changing one transaction changes the Merkle root, then its block header hash and the descendants’ required links. Which principle explains this?
checks.correct: Nonce supports work search; Merkle root commits transactions; prior hash links history
distractors: Nonce is the receiver’s private key
Merkle root stores every private password
Prior hash encrypts all previous transactions
checks.teach: Separate the miner’s search value, the transaction commitment, and the history link.
checks.answer: A proof-of-work nonce is a value miners vary while searching for a block-header hash meeting a target. A Merkle root commits to the block’s transactions using a tree of hashes. The previous-block hash links a block to its predecessor. Altering a transaction changes its commitment and invalidates later links unless recomputed. A toy rehash demonstration is not the full security model: distributed validation and cumulative proof of work make rewriting accepted history difficult.
checks.example: Changing one transaction changes the Merkle root, then its block header hash and the descendants’ required links.

checks.q: An owner attempts to spend the same output twice. Both signatures could be valid, but both transactions cannot be accepted in one valid history. Which principle explains this?
checks.correct: Signatures authorize, consensus orders, and rewards motivate participation
distractors: Hashing alone prevents all double spending
Miners can authorize spending anyone’s coins
checks.teach: Authorization does not establish which of two conflicting authorized spends came first; network agreement addresses that ordering problem.
checks.answer: Signatures demonstrate authorization to spend. Nodes check spending rules, including whether an output is unspent. Consensus orders transactions so competing spends do not both become accepted history. A block subsidy and fees incentivize miners. Public records use addresses or spending scripts rather than mandatory civil identities, but linked transactions can reveal relationships. This is pseudonymity. Nakamoto’s paper contrasts verification by cryptographic proof with the reversal costs, mediation, and trust demands of financial intermediaries.
checks.example: An owner attempts to spend the same output twice. Both signatures could be valid, but both transactions cannot be accepted in one valid history.

checks.q: A voice application may prioritize timely delivery over retransmitting old audio; a file transfer needs all bytes. Both rely on IP routing. Which principle explains this?
checks.correct: TCP reliable stream; UDP datagrams; IP best-effort routing
distractors: IP guarantees every byte in order
UDP is only allowed on private networks
TCP stands for Transportation Control Protocol
checks.teach: Reliability, latency tradeoffs, and routing are separate design concerns.
checks.answer: TCP provides a reliable ordered byte stream, using SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK for conventional connection establishment. UDP provides datagrams without TCP-style delivery or ordering guarantees and is useful where applications tolerate loss or implement their own recovery. Both operate at the transport layer. IP addresses and routes packets at the network layer with best-effort delivery. UDP is not restricted to private networks, and TCP does not guarantee timeliness or encryption. Packet lengths can vary.
checks.example: A voice application may prioritize timely delivery over retransmitting old audio; a file transfer needs all bytes. Both rely on IP routing.

checks.q: A name resolves unexpectedly, so an analyst checks DNS evidence and validation. Separate authentication logs and packet metadata help establish the incident timeline. Which principle explains this?
checks.correct: Different protocols handle naming, management, diagnostics, files, and email
distractors: FTP always uses port 20 for all traffic
ICMP is a mail retrieval service
checks.teach: Match each service to its job before memorizing associated names and port facts.
checks.answer: DNS resolves names and other records; poisoning supplies false resolution information. DNSSEC authenticates signed DNS data and integrity when correctly validated, without encrypting ordinary DNS queries. SNMP monitors and manages devices; v3 supports stronger protection. ICMP carries network control and diagnostic messages, including ping. Traditional FTP transfers files without encryption: port 21 controls, port 20 is traditionally active-mode data, while passive mode negotiates data ports. SMTP transfers mail and POP retrieves it. Wireshark analyzes packets; log correlation helps investigation.
checks.example: A name resolves unexpectedly, so an analyst checks DNS evidence and validation. Separate authentication logs and packet metadata help establish the incident timeline.

checks.q: A traveler sees two access points with the hotel’s name. The name alone cannot determine which is authorized. Which principle explains this?
checks.correct: Displayed names and addresses can be impersonated
